label: Concentrated Matrix Langevin Models
notes: This chapter studies the matrix Langevin family in the regime where its concentration parameter grows large. We motivate why a tight cluster of orientations on the Stiefel manifold behaves almost like a Gaussian, and we preview the linearization, the normalizing-constant expansion, and the matrix-normal inference target.

label: The Matrix Langevin Density
notes: We recall the matrix Langevin density on the Stiefel manifold, written through the trace of F transpose X. The matrix parameter F encodes both the modal orientation and the strength of concentration via its singular values, and the normalizing constant is a hypergeometric function of matrix argument.

label: Stiefel Manifold and Modal Orientation
notes: The Stiefel manifold collects orthonormal p-frames in n-dimensional space. The mode of the matrix Langevin density is the orientation aligned with the parameter, obtained from its polar part. Inference asks how sharply observed frames cluster around this modal orientation, which sets the concentration scale.

label: Low vs High Concentration
notes: At low concentration the sampled frames spread broadly, nearly uniformly, over the manifold. As the singular values of the parameter grow, the mass collapses into a tight cap around the mode. The high-concentration regime is exactly where local Gaussian approximation becomes accurate and useful.

label: The Concentration Parameter
notes: We separate the parameter into a modal orientation and a scalar concentration multiplying a fixed direction structure. Large concentration means large singular values, which means the exponent in the density decays steeply as a frame departs from the mode. This steep decay drives every asymptotic argument that follows.

label: Tangent Space at the Mode
notes: At the modal orientation we attach the tangent space to the Stiefel manifold. Tangent vectors satisfy a skew-symmetry constraint with the mode, giving the space its dimension. Local coordinates on this tangent plane will carry the linearized model and convert manifold inference into Euclidean inference.

label: Linearizing the Density
notes: We expand the trace exponent of the matrix Langevin density to second order in a tangent coordinate about the mode. The linear term vanishes because the mode is a stationary point, leaving a negative-definite quadratic form. Exponentiating that quadratic produces a Gaussian shape on the tangent space.

label: The Gaussian Approximation
notes: The leading local approximation is a matrix-normal law on the tangent coordinate, with covariance set by the inverse of the concentration-scaled Hessian. As concentration grows the approximation error shrinks, so the curved Stiefel problem is replaced by a flat matrix-normal problem near the mode.

label: Normalizing Constant Expansion
notes: The hypergeometric normalizing constant admits a high-concentration asymptotic expansion. The leading factor is the exponential of the summed singular values times a Gaussian-integral volume term, with polynomial corrections in inverse concentration. This expansion makes likelihoods and moments computable without evaluating the full hypergeometric series.

label: Matrix-Normal Inference
notes: Because the linearized model is matrix-normal, estimation of the modal orientation and concentration reduces to familiar Gaussian computations. The maximum likelihood estimate aligns with the sample mean frame, and the concentration is read from the spread of tangent residuals, giving closed-form approximate inference.

label: Diagnostic: Resultant Length
notes: A finite diagnostic tracks the norm of the mean resultant of sampled frames. Near uniformity it stays small; under strong concentration it approaches one. Watching this scalar as concentration varies confirms that the tight-cap regime, where the Gaussian approximation is trusted, has genuinely been entered.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We summarized the high-concentration matrix Langevin story: cluster tightly around the mode, linearize onto the tangent space, expand the normalizing constant, and inherit matrix-normal inference. These approximations underpin asymptotic tests and confidence regions and connect directly to the directional and tensor models studied next.
